newsitem.title: NEPAL: Seven ministers quit Nepal's government.
newsitem.headline: Seven ministers quit Nepal's government.

text.p: Nepali Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's tenuous grip on power appeared in jeopardy on Sunday after seven government ministers from a coalition partner quit and opposition communists demanded a no-confidence vote.

The Rastriya Parajatantra Party (RPP) said its leader in parliament had informed King Birendra in a letter that a faction of the party had withdrawn support for Deuba and that his 15-month-old government had lost its majority.

"The government has automatically run into minority and his majesty the king should initiate the constitutional process to set up a new government," RPP spokesman Kamal Thapa told a news conference in the capital Kathmandu.
The RPP and another minority partner, the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (SNSP), joined Deuba's Nepali Congress last year to topple a communist-led government in a no-confidence vote.
The Nepali Congress party is the main partner in the three-party coalition with 86 members in the 205-seat House of Representatives, or lower house.
The RPP, with 19 deputies, and the NSP with three had given the coalition a narrow majority in the house, which currently has 200 sitting members.
The opposition Communist United Marxist-Leninist (UML) party holds 87 seats.

The communists have offered to back a new government led by RPP parliamentary leader Lokendra Bahadur Chand, who claimed 11 of his party's 19 deputies backed the decision to withdraw support for Deuba.
Before the resignations, the RPP held 13 of 46 government portfolios.
Chand accused Nepali Congress of harassing his party's supporters and violating an agreement between the coalition partners. He did not elaborate.
RPP vice-president Padma Sundar Lawati resigned as agriculture minister on Friday after being charged with corruption over fertiliser deals.
RPP co-chairman Rajeswor Devkota said there was no direct link between the charges against Lawati and the decision to withdraw support for Deuba.

"But there are sufficient reasons to believe that Nepali Congress leaders were behind the move against Lawati," he told Reuters. "The Nepali Congress did not show good behaviour towards the coalition partners."
The RPP and Nepali Congress have had strained relations since Deuba assumed power in September last year.
In March, six RPP ministers resigned from the government, but they quickly patched up their differences with the government in time for Deuba to survive a no-confidence motion.
Chand said King Birendra had been asked to convene a special session of the lower house for a fresh no-confidence motion.
The communist UML party said the request was signed by 102 deputies, well over the minimum number.
